question.prompt:
Any three vertices of the cube \(PQRSTUVW,\) shown in the figure below, can be connected to form a triangle. (For example, vertices \(P,\) \(Q,\) and \(R\) can be connected to form isosceles \(\bigtriangleup PQR.\)) How many of these triangles are equilateral and contain \(P\) as a vertex?

[Figure 1](figures/2024_AMC_8_Q20_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
An equilateral triangle containing \(P\) must use two other vertices at the same distance from \(P\). Grouping the vertices by that distance reduces the number of pairs we need to check.

Let the cube's edge length be \(a>0\). By the Pythagorean theorem, every square face diagonal has squared length
\[
a^2+a^2=2a^2.
\]
Also, \(RU\) is perpendicular to the top face, so \(\triangle PRU\) is right at \(R\). Therefore
\[
PU^2=PR^2+RU^2=3a^2.
\]
The seven other vertices fall into three groups: \(Q,S,W\) have squared distance \(a^2\) from \(P\); \(R,T,V\) have squared distance \(2a^2\); and \(U\) has squared distance \(3a^2\). These distances are distinct because \(a>0\).

Choosing two vertices from \(Q,S,W\) does not work: the segment joining them is a face diagonal, longer than their distance \(a\) from \(P\). The single vertex \(U\) cannot supply a pair.

Every pair from \(R,T,V\) does work. The segments \(RT,RV,TV\) are face diagonals too, so each resulting triangle has three equal sides. The three unordered pairs give exactly
\[
\triangle PRT,\qquad \triangle PRV,\qquad \triangle PTV.
\]
Every possible pair has been covered, and each listed pair gives one distinct triangle. Thus there are \(\boxed{3}\) triangles, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Group vertices by their distance from P
